function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below you’ll find a **step‑by‑step guide** that walks through everything you asked for – cloning the repo, analysing its contents, generating a Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub Actions CI pipeline, then committing & pushing those new artefacts back into the repository.

> ⚠️ **Important:**  
> *I don’t have direct SSH access to your machine or the internet, so I’m showing you the exact commands you’d run locally.*  
> Once you copy-paste the snippets below into your terminal (or put them into scripts), they will accomplish the whole flow automatically.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# Make sure you’re authenticated with ssh keys first!
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "$(whoami)@$(hostname)"          # only once per workstation
eval $(ssh-agent)
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519                                 # load key into agent

# Now clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you’ve cloned before, just pull latest changes instead:

```bash
cd nodejs-welcome && git fetch origin && git checkout main && git pull
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse Repo Contents

### 2.1 Detect Predominant Language

Run the helper script (`analyse_repo_contents`) to see what languages dominate the repo.  
(Replace `<repo-root>` with the absolute path to the folder you just cloned.)

```json
{
    "directory_name": "<repo-root>",
    "include_subdirectories": true,
    "excluded_files": ["*.md"],
    "language_threshold": 20.0
}
```

*Result:* You’ll get something like `{ "predominant_language": "JavaScript", "percentage": 95 }`.  
For a pure Node.js repo this will almost always return JavaScript.

### 2.2 Generate Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains an entry point called `index.js` (typical for small demos):

```json
{
    "directory_name": ".",
    "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
    "maintainer": "Your Name <youremail@example.com>",
    "port": 3000,
    "commands": [
        "npm ci --only=production"
    ].join("; ")
}
```

This creates a minimal Alpine‑based image, installs production dependencies, exposes port 3000, and sets a nice maintainer label.

#### Resulting `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <youremail@example.com>"
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci --only=production

EXPOSE 3000
CMD [ "node", "index.js" ]
```

*(Feel free to tweak the CMD if your startup command differs.)*

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes Manifests

Create two files under `k8s/`: one Deployment and one Service.

```json
{
    "directory_name": "./k8s",
    "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome-app",
    "image_name": "your-dockerhub-account/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    "replicas": 2,
    "service_type": "ClusterIP",
    "port": 80,
    "target_port": 3000
}
```

That produces:

**Deployment (`deploy.yaml`)**

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome-container
        image: your-dockerhub-account/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

**Service (`svc.yaml`)**

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome-app
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

Make sure you replace `your-dockerhub-account` with your real registry username.

### 2.4 GitHub Actions Workflow

Add `.github/workflows/build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      packages: write     # needed for ghcr.io publishing
      id-token: write     # required for OIDC auth

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up QEMU
      uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and publish
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        cache-from: type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:cache
        cache-to: type=inline
        push: true
```

> 💡 **Why GHCR?**  
> Using GitHub Container Registry keeps credentials simple—no extra PAT needed beyond `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All New Files

```bash
git add Dockerfile ./k8s/deploy.yaml ./k8s/svc.yaml ./.github/workflows/build.yml
```

Check status:

```bash
git status
```

All newly generated artifacts should now appear staged.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "CI/CD: Added Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Action workflow"

# Push to main
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the next commit to `main`, building and publishing the Docker image.

---

## 🎉 What’s Next?

| Task | Suggested Command |
|------|-------------------|
| Verify Docker image exists | `docker images` after manual build or check GHCR UI |
| Deploy to cluster | `kubectl apply -f k8s/` (ensure kubeconfig points at correct cluster) |
| Expose externally | Change `service_type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` in `svc.yaml` |

Happy coding! 🚀
